chunks.text: Peltophorum pterocarpum — known as the yellow flame, copperpod, yellow poinciana or yellow-flamboyant — is a Fabaceae tree native to tropical Southeast Asia and northern Australasia, first formally described in 1825. It is usually 15-25 m tall (occasionally to 50 m), with bipinnate leaves 30-60 cm long made up of 16-20 pinnae and 20-40 small oval leaflets each, and large compound racemes of bright yellow flowers up to 20 cm long that appear in a 'mass flowering' display, typically from about four years of age onward. Its pods are flat, 5-10 cm long, red when young and ripening to black. Beyond ornamental planting — it is commonly used in India, Pakistan, Nigeria and parts of the United States (Florida, Hawaii), often set alternately with the scarlet-flowered Delonix regia to create a contrasting red-and-yellow avenue effect — it has genuine commercial and cultural uses: its timber goes into cabinet-making, its foliage serves as fodder, and the characteristic brown dye (sogan) used in inland Javanese batik is derived from this species. In Telangana it is used decoratively in the Batukamma festival.

chunks.source: NParks Singapore — Flora & Fauna Web (Peltophorum pterocarpum, 'Yellow Flame')
chunks.text: Singapore's National Parks Board profile adds an important local wrinkle: although Peltophorum pterocarpum is native to Singapore, it is listed there as Critically Endangered in the wild, even as it remains one of the island's most widely planted roadside and park trees, grown up to 35 m with an open, umbrella-shaped crown 9-12 m wide. This gap between wild rarity and ubiquitous cultivation is a recurring pattern for ornamental native species in heavily urbanised Singapore, and the tree's drought resistance and tolerance of alkaline, clay, saline and salt-spray soils have made it especially well suited to the island's hot, exposed roadside conditions, where it is propagated by seed, grafting or branch cuttings and raised in nurseries for about a year before field planting. Its bright yellow, insect-pollinated flowers with orange stamens and a reddish-brown central mark bloom mainly from March to May with a smaller second flush from September to November, and its bark, leaves and wood contain tannins used to dye leather and, in Java, for batik. Two individual trees have been formally recognised as Heritage Trees under Singapore's conservation programme.
